title: ‘Nothing About This Was Inevitable’
summary: The second floor of OpenAI’s old headquarters had a theme. Each room was named after one of the most important inventions in human history: “Clock,” “Fire,” and, of course, “AGI,” or artificial general intelligence. I saw this in the spring of 2024, when I was interviewing some of the company’s rese...
content:
The second floor of OpenAI’s old headquarters had a theme. Each room was named after one of the most important inventions in human history: “Clock,” “Fire,” and, of course, “AGI,” or artificial general intelligence. I saw this in the spring of 2024, when I was interviewing some of the company’s researchers about recent technical advances. At the time, ChatGPT was still making embarrassing arithmetic errors, and the notion that the bot would ever rival human intelligence was dubious. But here, in the renovated shell of a former mayonnaise factory in San Francisco, AGI’s arrival was predestined.

This belief in AGI—a computer program with capabilities that rival or even exceed those of the human mind—is foundational to the mission of Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic, three of the most influential AI companies in the world. And the pursuit of that milestone is the subject of The AGI Chronicles, a new book by the tech reporter and Atlantic contributing writer Kevin Roose, which he describes as his attempt to document the decade “when the human monopoly on advanced intelligence ended, and a new world was born.” Roose, a prominent and well-connected commenter on the AI boom, follows the internecine world of the frontier AI companies in remarkable, at times almost insular, detail. Based on interviews with more than 150 researchers, executives, investors, and policy makers close to the technology’s development, The AGI Chronicles traces crucial moments across DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic from 2015 through early 2026 to figure out how we got to this very messy moment in AI, and who’s responsible for what happens next.

[Read: The singularity is not what it seems]

If you scan statements from executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, there is a sense of fatalism about the rise of AI. In my conversation with Amodei last year, he likened developing AI to operating an out-of-control bus: It can’t be stopped or even slowed, but perhaps it can be steered. In an interview last month, Altman called AI “an inevitability.” According to this framing, AI executives are simply conductors, doing their best to provide guardrails for an era that’s careering our way, whether anyone likes it or not. Roose’s book prompted me to consider a question that is often neglected in the mile-a-minute news cycle: Are the leading AI companies simply heralding an inevitable evolution of this technology, as many of them claim, or are they directing that advancement? The answer will have tremendous bearing on how we assign responsibility for the world taking shape around us.

The AGI Chronicles is of both minds on the topic. On the one hand, Roose is very explicit that he is archiving decisions made by a small group of people. “AGI was not inevitable,” he writes, but “invented, developed, and commercialized by a few hundred people.” On the other hand, sometimes the book reads like a natural history, describing a procession of events outside the control of any specific group of people, an almost geologic force sweeping the planet as “a new world was born.” He notes how, throughout the years, various companies and officials had yet to “wake up.” By 2024, he writes, “the idea of going back to the old world, to a time before all this, seemed more delusional than expecting the exponential to continue.”

At times, Roose’s book echoes the loss of agency professed by AI executives. Of course, the inevitability of any one outcome is a self-serving fabrication. There is no prophecy that a handful of Silicon Valley companies dictating their own rules, running roughshod over copyright law and environmental regulations while mucking up once-reliable internet services with AI features nobody asked for, will operate largely unencumbered. Industries take shape through decisions made by individual actors and investors, the collective desire of the public, and the action or inaction of regulators.

If you look to the late 1800s, for example, it would have seemed likely that electric cars would dominate the market in the following century. America’s best-selling car in 1897 was electric, and in the 1910s, Henry Ford was trying to develop an electric car with Thomas Edison. But a series of technological limitations and human decisions—including various financial missteps and harsh criticism from advocates of petrol-powered cars—changed the course of history, leaving a legacy that we’re reckoning with more than a century later.

In the 1950s, it seemed as if nuclear reactors were destined to dot the nation and power the future. But a series of political campaigns and spectacular errors—the anti-nuclear movement, Three Mile Island, Chernobyl—crushed the nuclear age before it ever really started. Then there was the Space Age and supersonic flight—there are so many seemingly inevitable technological eras that never quite made it, not so much because of technology itself as because of political and economic choices. There are, similarly, so many corporate behemoths—Standard Oil, Kodak, Bear Stearns—that, because of regulation or complacency or fraud, unraveled. The inverse holds for many technologies and companies considered inevitable today: Different regulatory environments, international agreements, or priorities for Pentagon labs could have stopped the development of an open and global internet, smartphones, social media.

When I recently called Roose to discuss his book and ask what he made of the industry’s frequently prophetic tone, he initially told me he believes that “nothing about this was inevitable. These were decisions made by people.” But he then said that he wanted to “complicate” that: “Once scaling the transformer worked, and once the scaling laws were documented,” Roose said, “I think it was inevitable that the companies building this stuff would push it as far as they possibly could.”

I’d like to further complicate that view. Beyond the urge to test the bounds of any technology and reap enormous profits, the industry has been shaped by very human decisions. AI researchers chose to train their models on troves of copyrighted works without seeking permission, leading to countless creators suddenly getting left out of the economic equation. OpenAI chose to rush a free-to-use ChatGPT to the market in late 2022, kicking off a hype cycle and a subsequent investment bonanza. Venture-capital, private-equity, and tech firms chose to sink untold billions into a still-unprofitable technology. Data-center developers chose to eschew solar panels in favor of combustion turbines, which they perceive as faster and more reliable. On the government side, Donald Trump has chosen to ignore or eliminate any substantive federal regulation of AI. An industry that negotiated royalty payments, prioritized clean energy, gave itself longer development cycles, or faced serious federal regulation might look entirely different.

The question of inevitability and responsibility may sound arcane, but it has real ramifications. In the Bay Area, tied up with the myth of AI’s inevitability is a sort of spiritual devotion: “Thank you to the machines, and the structure of reality, for letting us understand a little more,” Altman wrote on X this week. The more you treat AI as inevitable, the more it seems like a cosmic force rather than a product resulting from industrial and commercial design choices. The more you treat AI as inevitable, the less you can hold any company or person responsible for things going wrong. The executives, in this view, are only fractionally more empowered than us in deciding what happens next; more important, everyone else needs to wake up. As Altman put it to Politico earlier this month, “The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”

In the months since Roose concluded his reporting, the AI industry and its products have risen to still-greater global prominence and triggered even greater fears. When I asked him what new chapters he might add if he were still writing, Roose said that he would end the book with the recent White House press conference in which Trump, Amodei, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Elon Musk, and several other tech executives addressed AI-safety concerns. He recalled a speech Amodei gave in Anthropic’s early days about how different parts of society would gradually become attuned to the transformative effects of this technology, beginning with AI firms and ending with the state. It felt, Roose told me, “like the prophecy had been fulfilled.”

title: Trump’s Team of Mercenaries
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.Kimberly Guilfoyle was so close to getting it right.The Trump hanger-on—former fiancée to Don Jr. and t...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Kimberly Guilfoyle was so close to getting it right.

The Trump hanger-on—former fiancée to Don Jr. and the current ambassador to Greece—was exchanging messages with a man named Eric Deters, according to a bombshell Wall Street Journal story last night. Deters, a right-wing podcast host, failed political candidate, and suspended lawyer in Kentucky, wanted help in clearing up some tax issues, and also wanted the Trump administration to extradite a doctor whose alleged fraud victims he was advising in a legal case. Guilfoyle, the messages indicate, wanted money—in one instance, a $100,000 wire—and she wanted it untraceable.

Guilfoyle was right to worry about secrecy. She was about to begin confirmation hearings for her ambassadorship, and understood the pay-to-play could hurt her. Yet neither she nor Deters could stop breaking the Stringer Bell rule by recording their skullduggery in writing.

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” Guilfoyle wrote. “Please.” And in another: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” Yet even as she laid these instructions out, she kept haranguing Deters for indiscretion. “I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on signal,” she wrote, referring to the encrypted messaging app. In one message, she wrote, “If you write an email or a text about, l’m gonna kill you cause I love you but you’re so out of control.” Unfortunately for Guilfoyle, her Signal messages were not as safe a space as she might have wished. (The Journal does not reveal how it viewed the messages. Guilfoyle’s lawyer broadly disputed their authenticity to the paper but offered no details.)

Somehow, this is not the only Trump scandal with Balkan ties in the news this week. The New York Times reported that James Blair and Chris LaCivita, who are ostensibly President Trump’s top political advisers, traveled—during an intense midterm campaign in which Republicans appear to be on the verge of serious setbacks—to advise a candidate in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s self-governing Serbian entity.

Both of these stories show the way that many people in Trump’s orbit view their positions not as public service but as a profit center. There’s a long and often depressing pattern of former officials capitalizing on government and political work, but Trump’s aides aren’t even willing to wait until they take their leave to start taking. Forget a team of rivals. Trump world is a team of mercenaries, in some cases literally.

Jared Kushner, who was a senior adviser in his first presidency and is married to his daughter Ivanka, continues to work as an envoy for Trump while pursuing business deals around the world. As Dexter Filkins wrote in The New Yorker in September, Kushner’s record as a diplomat is underwhelming, yet his financial gains have been enormous. “He represents a new kind of Washington figure, for whom public office serves as a means to extraordinary wealth,” Filkins wrote. Kushner and Ivanka Trump even have their own Balkan boondoggle, an attempt to develop an island in Albania that has run into legal and political difficulties.

Earlier this year, the Times reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick helped negotiate access to Kazakh tungsten reserves for an American mining company, and the federal government provided $1.6 billion in financing. Lutnick’s sons and Trump’s sons are both involved with companies that stand to profit from the deal (though representatives for them have said that they did not play a role in the deal). A Washington Post investigation this summer noted that Trump’s sons have invested heavily in defense-technology companies; the companies have scored “at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested and an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options.” (Company representatives told the Post that they secured their business without assistance from Trump’s sons.)

Where do any of these people get the idea that this is appropriate or that they can get away with it? From the president himself, naturally. Trump has moved on from small-scale grifts such as charging the Secret Service exorbitant fees to stay in his hotels during his first term to far more ambitious and lucrative schemes such as crypto ventures; even conservative estimates put his gains during this term alone in the billions.

Though Trump doesn’t have ethical scruples, he does have a sense of right and wrong: It’s right for him to profiteer, but wrong for others to make too much money from his name. That’s where Blair, LaCivita, and Guilfoyle may run into trouble. Politico reports that Republicans’ “knives are now fully out” for the two consultants. Trump himself weighed in on Truth Social, saying he was unaware of their clients but adding that he “will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Firing them just before the midterms seems risky, as it might just create more chaos for Republicans, but they could make for good scapegoats after the fact. Trump has not spoken publicly about the Guilfoyle story, although Vice President Vance said he didn’t “love that.” In a further embarrassment, the article emerged while Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting Athens.

Perhaps inevitably, Guilfoyle’s relationship with Deters ended acrimoniously. “I have paid you $300,000 over the years,” he wrote her in 2025, adding, in an amusingly self-negating flourish, “As of this memo, I have not received one favor. I am not naive or a sucker.” She was not happy, either. “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” she told him at one point, per the Journal. Her warning may have been too late.

Today’s News

  1. U.S. prosecutors charged Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, with conspiring to torture Americans and other prisoners in Venezuela to suppress opposition and maintain power. The new charge has been added to the federal case against the couple, who are scheduled for trial in June 2027.
  2. At least 30 people were killed in a Russian strike on a bus in eastern Ukraine, a day after another Russian strike killed 22 people in an apartment building. The attacks come as Russia intensifies its use of drones, missiles, and guided bombs against Ukrainian targets.
  3. Hurricane Isaias strengthened into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season as it approached the Gulf Coast, and landfall is expected as soon as tomorrow. It could reach Category 3 strength, prompting hurricane watches and mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida.

Evening Read

Illlustration by Hannah Robinson

Forgive the Bad Texters

By Julie Beck

Whenever I receive a text, this is what happens. I pick up my phone. So far, so good. I experience whatever emotion the message elicits—the pleasant warmth of being reached out to, possibly the annoyance of being interrupted. Then, if conditions are right, if I’m not too busy or in the middle of talking with someone else, if my mind is at peace, if my anxiety is at no more than a low hum, if Mercury is not in retrograde, I will respond right then and there. If conditions are not right, it will be as though the text never existed at all.

Read the full article.

title: Anne Carson’s Seductive Strangeness
summary: Anne Carson, who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature today, doesn’t write masterpieces or door-stoppers, and she has no interest in emulating the great works of the past—including those of past laureates. Despite her training as a classicist and her celebrated skill as a translator, she would lik...
content:
Anne Carson, who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature today, doesn’t write masterpieces or door-stoppers, and she has no interest in emulating the great works of the past—including those of past laureates. Despite her training as a classicist and her celebrated skill as a translator, she would likely have little to say about the authenticity of film adaptations of The Odyssey. Carson is a poet by trade, but she’s really an archaeologist of sorts, sifting through the pottery shards of culture and letting the light of our own time illuminate their beauty.

Carson prefers to use fragments as seeds for her own poetry, and the high-cultural touchpoints for her lyrics and critical essays—Sappho, Samuel Beckett, Franz Kafka, Michelangelo Antonioni, Simone Weil—sometimes give her work an air of forbidding experimentation that quickly turns, upon reading, into pleasure and delight. You may not know or care who Heloïse and Abelard are, but I can promise that you will enjoy reading them argue in a hotel room in the middle of her 2005 “spoken-word opera,” Decreation.

Across roughly two dozen translations and original books, a twee-punk “don’t give a damn” attitude pervades Carson’s reinterpretation of ancient texts: Her poetry shuns obeisance to tradition and literality and embraces creative fantasy instead. For that reason, the barrier to entry for her poetry is surprisingly low—surprisingly, I mean, for a poet whose books often contain a page or two of footnotes. Carson wrote a Ph.D. dissertation on the ancient poet Sappho at the University of Toronto, in the city where she was born in 1950. When I was a classics major in college, her 1998 re-creation of a bit of obscure Greek mythology, Autobiography of Red, was a cult object. Some of her poetry isn’t even poetry at all, but a mix of essays, screenplays, even the odd oratorio. Nox, her 2010 elegy for her brother—the title is Latin for “night”—arrives in a box and unfolds like an accordion. Carson’s predilection for the classics doesn’t domesticate them; it riffs on how astonishingly strange it can be to put words down on a page (or papyrus) in a meaningful order, and to try to have them capture the human condition.

[Read: The best American poetry of the 21st century (so far)]

Sappho, Carson’s early subject, offers an important clue as to why her work matters to us now, and perhaps also as to why she won the Nobel. Sappho’s poetry has survived only in bits and pieces, and her form of writing, as much as her obsession with love and longing, has inspired Carson’s own iconoclastic, restless tacking among genres. Yet Carson is averse to the common assumption that we have to look for what’s directly relatable in the past in order to fall in love with it. In an interview with The Paris Review, she confessed that she finds very little “direct relevance of ancient things to modern things”; instead, she gets “little glimpses of similarity, embedded in unbelievable otherness.”

That strikes me as pretty close to a definition of poetry itself, the art form that may be better than any other at embedding everyday objects (a wheelbarrow, a coffee spoon) within the tantalizing atmosphere of the new. Carson’s poetry connects us to the past for the same reason that it stands out as some of the most accomplished poetry of her generation: Rather than lulling us with history’s familiarity, she seduces us with its strangeness.

In the days leading up to the Nobel Prize announcement, I happened to have been rereading Autobiography of Red for the first time in 24 years. This “novel in verse” takes its prompt from a 6th-century-B.C.E. fragment about a little monster, Geryon, who falls in love with Herakles—before the god kills him. In Carson’s rendering, the two meet as teenagers at a bus station and reunite years later in Buenos Aires. They travel by plane to a volcano in Peru, where Geryon, now an aspiring photographer, takes pictures of the bubbling lava (no one dies). From so fragile, bizarre, and slender a source—we never forget this is a meet-cute between a red, winged monster and a divine hero—Carson conjures a romance in which love feels unbelievably alien and yet utterly recognizable: “Up on the overpass / the night was wide open / and blowing headlights like a sea. He stood against the wind and let it peel him / clean.”

Carson’s playfulness, humor, and curiosity—and, above all, her tenderness—make her poetry a powerful antidote to the chilled and coarsened social world of the present, not to mention the worry that history and the classics will lose their audiences. What I find most moving about her work is her ability to turn abstract thought into concrete feeling, and to make this feeling our own. Who has not wondered, as the young Geryon does, what “distance” looks like? Carson writes, “It extends from a spaceless within to the edge of what can be loved.” When I gaze down a path or a road, when I feel the separation from someone I love, or when I think of the gulf between the present and the past, I somehow know exactly what she means.

title: The Oil Crisis America Saw Coming
summary: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.In December 1987, The Atlantic had some reassuring news for readers: The next oil crisis didn’t have to happen.The United States had already endured the oil shocks of the...
content:
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.

In December 1987, The Atlantic had some reassuring news for readers: The next oil crisis didn’t have to happen.

The United States had already endured the oil shocks of the 1970s, and Amory B. Lovins and L. Hunter Lovins, a pair of then-married environmentalists, argued in this magazine that the country had learned from the experience. The U.S. had diversified its sources of foreign oil, and the American economy needed less oil to grow, a shift that the Lovinses attributed mainly to efficiency gains, such as better-insulated buildings and more fuel-efficient cars. Oil production had grown outside OPEC, an organization of oil-exporting states, reducing the world’s reliance on Persian Gulf oil. Even the Strait of Hormuz, a flash point in the Iran-Iraq War of the ’80s, appeared less threatening to the global supply. By 1987, less oil was passing through the waterway than earlier in the decade, and the Lovinses believed that reserves and alternative routes could help make up for any sudden cutoffs caused by geopolitical tensions.

The moment offered what the writers called a “unique opportunity”: a reprieve from Middle Eastern dominance of the global oil supply. “If this interval is frittered away,” they warned, “it could end with the United States, its alternative options expired, needing Middle Eastern oil more than ever.”

Nearly four decades later, America is far less vulnerable to foreign-oil disruptions, but it is once again caught in a global oil crisis, and the Strait of Hormuz is back at the center. Before the Iran war, about a quarter of the world’s maritime oil passed through the strait, roughly three times the daily volume that had passed through in 1987. The effective closure of the waterway has resulted in global oil inventories falling by more than 500 million barrels since February, and Americans are feeling the effects, as the costs of diesel, air travel, food, and other goods all rise.

But not all of the Lovinses’ worries have come to pass. America has become far less reliant on foreign oil than it was in the ’80s; the shale boom, precipitated by advances in horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, unlocked large amounts of domestic oil, transforming the U.S. energy market beginning in the 2000s. Last year, American crude production reached a record 13.6 million barrels a day, and Persian Gulf countries supplied just 8 percent of U.S. crude imports. The contrast with the 1970s is stark: In 1977, the broader group of OPEC countries supplied 85 percent of American crude-oil imports. As my colleague Rogé Karma reported in March, America’s growing energy independence appears to have helped convince the Trump administration ahead of the Iran war that the U.S. could withstand a disruption in the Persian Gulf. “We don’t get any oil anymore out of the Strait of Hormuz,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said last October, in defense of America’s decision to strike Iran’s nuclear facilities earlier that year.

The Lovinses had imagined a different route to energy security. They called it “substitution”: reducing the need for oil overall by continuing to improve energy efficiency in buildings and vehicles, and replacing oil with natural gas or alternative fuels. They argued that efficiency could buy the country time to free itself from dependence on foreign oil. America ultimately achieved much of that goal, but by producing more oil rather than using less. After OPEC’s 1973 oil embargo, President Richard Nixon launched “Project Independence” with the goal of reducing the country’s reliance on foreign oil. Congress adopted new conservation measures, and Jimmy Carter made reducing energy consumption a centerpiece of his presidency, while also beginning to lift federal controls on oil prices to free up more domestic production. In 1979, Carter went so far as to promise that the country would never again “use more foreign oil” than it had in 1977. Days after taking office, President Ronald Reagan eliminated the remaining federal controls on oil prices. The approach appeared to be working: By the early 1980s, U.S. oil consumption had fallen to its lowest level in more than a decade.

But the conditions that encouraged conservation soon changed. Weaker oil demand and growing supply contributed to a glut that sent oil prices plunging in 1986. As oil became cheaper, the economic pressure to conserve diminished, and the efficiency gains of the previous decade began to level off. The political approach was changing too. Reagan’s administration sought deep cuts to federal conservation research, part of a broader retreat from government-led energy programs during the 1980s.

Conservation had never been the country’s only answer to the oil shocks. Policy makers were simultaneously trying to increase domestic production and diversify the country’s energy supply. Carter argued in 1979 that the country needed to “produce more” as well as “conserve more.” What ultimately endured was not the ambition to wean the country off oil, but the goal of making America less vulnerable to foreign suppliers.

In April, my colleague Idrees Kahloon wrote that the country is at a point where it can administer energy “shocks to other countries without feeling much pain itself,” but Americans have not been spared the effects of an international oil shortage. Gasoline prices still rise with global oil prices, regardless of where the crude comes from. Countries that are more dependent on Gulf energy, meanwhile, have borne more of the disruption. Most of the crude oil passing through Hormuz was headed to Asia, not the United States. The Philippines declared a state of emergency in response to energy shortages, Japan faced higher oil costs, and European countries saw disruptions to natural-gas shipments push prices up.

This is not quite the future the Lovinses imagined, but neither is it the one they feared. They understood the calm of the 1980s as a reprieve, not a resolution. Four decades later, the United States has emerged from the crises of the ’70s as the world’s largest oil producer, far less dependent on the Middle East but still dependent on fuel itself. America may not be as vulnerable to disruptions abroad, but as long as oil is traded on a global market, the country cannot fully insulate itself from what happens beyond its borders.

title: What I Saw at New York’s Anti-Israel October 7 Rallies
summary: Yesterday was a reminder of the difficulty that the pro-Palestine left has with showing grace even for the dead. On the third anniversary of the day that Hamas gunmen and freelance killers arrived in Israel on motorcycles and paragliders and trucks, and slaughtered children and grandparents and moth...
content:
Yesterday was a reminder of the difficulty that the pro-Palestine left has with showing grace even for the dead. On the third anniversary of the day that Hamas gunmen and freelance killers arrived in Israel on motorcycles and paragliders and trucks, and slaughtered children and grandparents and mothers and fathers and dancing young people, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani put out a statement that was empathetic and modulated in tone … for about 50 words.

“This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers,” Mamdani began. “It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.”

Alas, then came the next 162 words, as the young mayor indulged his anger with Israel. He apparently felt obligated to give New York City—which is home to the biggest Jewish population of any city on the globe—a history lesson that seemed to suggest that Israel brought the October 7 tragedy upon itself.

“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he wrote. “It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing.”

[Jonathan Chait: Progressive activists are sometimes on the wrong side of history]

On he went, referencing Israeli war crimes and apartheid and unbearable grief and American complicity in it all. By the time he concluded, he had turned grace into a cudgel. Ammiel Hirsch, a prominent New York rabbi and a longtime peace advocate, called the statement “morally perverse” and likened it to “sticking a knife into the pain of the Jewish community.”

Mamdani might have thought his statement to be provocative enough to satisfy even the most anti-Zionist, anti-Israel leftist. But portions of New York’s pro-Palestine community were insistent about observing the anniversary with a Citywide Protest Resisting Genocide since 1948. They were less intent on remembering Palestinians who have suffered grievously than they were focused on implicitly saluting Hamas’s savage attack, as their call to protest offered “glory to the martyrs, victory to the resistance.” And a fringe went further still, denouncing Mamdani for what it perceived as insufficient anti-Israel fervor.

I spent some hours yesterday tracking these protests, including classroom walkouts and marches, and in truth, the numbers were deeply underwhelming. The demonstration began with 80 or so New York University students gathering for a noontime rally in Washington Square Park. They chanted, denounced their university leaders, and listened as an NYU professor spun out various conspiracy theories suggesting that Israel was principally responsible for its own casualties. Two hours later, another 75 or 80 students gathered on Broadway, outside the Columbia University campus, and chanted, “Intifada revolution” and “Palestine from river to sea,” an idea that, as a practical matter, would entail the abolition of Israel.

A larger rally was planned at City Hall Park in the late afternoon. Protesters there numbered—and my grading could be generous—a touch more than 200. This included a breakaway group of roughly two dozen anti-Zionist ultra-Orthodox Satmars, a crew of black-clad anarchists who did their best to appear forbidding, and an impressively insistent Maoist Communist faction. The lackluster turnout might have owed in part to the fact that the grandees of New York’s organized left, in particular the New York City chapter of Democratic Socialists of America, were savvy enough to avoid militant protest on this solemn day. The New York City DSA went silent on social media, making no mention of October 7 or the rallies. Only the youth wing of DSA showed up.

[Rose Horowitch: Where are all the campus protests?]

There was a faint hint of anti-Mamdanism. A young protester, his face wrapped in a keffiyeh, shouted into a bullhorn and assayed a brief attack on the mayor. His voice was muffled by the cloth, so it was difficult to make out what he said, save for the fact that he repeated it rhythmically. Perhaps seven or eight protesters joined in, and a Maoist held aloft and jiggled an anti-Mamdani sign.

The atmosphere grew more hostile as day turned to night and the protest came to a desultory end. According to news reports, a rump group of perhaps 100 followers of various obscure militant-left groups and pro-Palestine groups marched north from city hall to Union Square. They were intent on disrupting a remembrance run by the anti-war group Israelis for Peace and attended by Mamdani. That vigil recognized both the Israeli dead and the many thousands of Palestinians who have died in the war in Gaza. The protesters crowded in, unleashing boos and chants, not least at Mamdani, whom they appeared to cast as Judas for standing alongside left-wing Jews and very liberal Zionists.

Peter Sterne, an editor at City & State New York, posted on X some of their nastier chants: “Traitor, traitor, come on out! You sold all your people out!” and “Zohran, you can’t hide. We charge you with genocide!” Mamdani, accompanied by his police detail, left to a chorus of jeers and boos.

A revolution eating its own is a historical commonplace. For now, Mamdani has used his considerable political skills to keep the most uncompromising of his pro-Palestine-left supporters in check. But last night perhaps signaled a fraying of patience.

title: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray

content:
Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.

content:
Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday

Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.

This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.

content:
Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again

As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
